summary: A planner and an improviser who turn up in a crisis, but let small things pile up because Emily keeps them quiet and Lucas moves on fast.

eras.title: All in
eras.line: About 370 messages a month, half of the replies inside five minutes, and a 403-day streak that started the week you met.

eras.title: The first hard year
eras.line: You moved in and Lucas started his company. Friction nearly tripled, and getting back to warm after a row took about six hours.

eras.title: Finding your rhythm
eras.line: Fewer messages but warmer ones, more plans made weeks ahead, and repair down to about three and a half hours.

a.basis: Emily sends most of the bookings, reminders and check-ins, but her warmest messages come the day after an evening Lucas cleared just for her. She says she is tired about once a month; he says it most weeks.

b.basis: Lucas praises Emily in words more often than anything else he sends her, and his longest, happiest replies follow her cheering on one of his plans.

truths.title: When it's hard, you turn up
truths.detail: You met 11 of 12 hard moments in your messages with real support, often within the hour. Emily turns up with a plan and practical help; Lucas turns up with words and a way through. Between you, the person having the hard day gets both kinds of help.

evidence.what: Lucas drove across town at 11pm when Emily's car broke down
Lucas cleared his week when Emily's grandmother was in hospital
Emily cleared a whole weekend for Lucas's investor pitch

truths.title: Fine, until it isn't
truths.detail: Emily says it's fine to keep the peace, and Lucas takes her at her word and moves on. The issue goes quiet, then comes back days later, bigger and about something else. Nine of your 23 rows about chores were an earlier one coming back.

evidence.what: a row about a missed dinner that came back two weeks later
five messages from Lucas, then a short okay from Emily
Emily asked for an hour and came back with what she needed

truths.title: What Emily wants isn't what she gives
truths.detail: Lucas guessed that Emily feels most loved when things are done for her, because that is how she shows love. What she actually wants most is unhurried time together. Her warmest messages come after quiet evenings for two, not after group plans or favours.

evidence.what: a quiet week at home Emily later called one of her best
Lucas fixed the boiler, and Emily replied with a thumbs-up
a phone-free Sunday walk, and Emily's longest message that month

close.takeaway: You both care a lot, but not always in the form the other needs. Lucas: give time, not just favours. Emily: say what you need, out loud.

appreciation.seen: One of you feels fully appreciated; the other mostly does.

evidence.insight: Emily's work is mostly invisible, so it's rarely thanked.
evidence.support: Emily made 60 plans in 2025 (trips, dinners, bookings); about 1 in 3 got a thank-you in words.

evidence.insight: Lucas thanks Emily for outcomes, not for the effort behind them.
evidence.support: Of his 520 messages of thanks since 2022, most follow an event, such as a great dinner, not the planning that made it happen.

appreciation.means: Emily does a lot of quiet work and, as her Psyche shows, tends to keep count without saying so. Lucas is grateful but thanks the result, not the work, so the effort goes unseen and a small resentment can build.

next.do: Lucas: once this week, thank Emily for the work behind something, not just for the thing.
next.because: her Psyche shows she does the unassigned work and keeps quiet about it.

next.do: Emily: when something feels unthanked, say so the same day, lightly.
next.because: her Psyche shows she tallies quietly rather than asking.

evidence.insight: Emily gives practical help but wants time. Lucas gives words and wants words back.
evidence.support: Emily's warmest messages follow 9 of 10 evenings alone together; Lucas's longest replies follow praise for his plans, across 2022 to 2026.

loves.means: Words are a match: Emily already knows they matter to Lucas, and she uses them. The gap runs the other way. Lucas reads Emily's acts of service as her love language, so he tends to show love by doing favours, when what fills her up is his undivided time.

next.do: Lucas: one evening a week with phones away and nothing planned after.
next.because: time together is how Emily feels most cared for, and Lucas guessed otherwise.

next.do: Emily: keep naming what you admire in Lucas; it lands every time.
next.because: words are how Lucas feels most cared for.

connection.seen: Making time for each other feels easier for one of you than the other.

evidence.insight: Small bids land most of the time, but not on weeknights.
evidence.support: Of 120 small bids in the messages read, 96 got a warm reply. 15 of the 21 missed were on weeknights, between 5pm and 8pm.

connection.means: Turning toward each other 80 times in 100 is good. The misses are not about care; they come at one time of day, when both of you are still in work mode and a small share gets a one-word reply.

next.do: Between 5pm and 8pm, if you can't reply properly, say you'll answer later, then do.
next.because: 15 of the 21 missed bids were on weeknight evenings.

missed.text: a photo of a new running route that got a thumbs-up and nothing else
news of a new client, met with a question about groceries

evidence.insight: You're better at hard times than good news.
evidence.support: You met 11 of 12 hard moments with real support, but only 7 of 11 pieces of good news with real interest.

counts.means: When one of you is struggling, the other turns up. Good news gets less: a quick well done, then back to logistics. How a partner reacts to good news builds as much closeness as support in hard times, and it is the easier one to fix.

next.do: When the other shares good news, ask two questions about it before changing the subject.
next.because: 4 of 11 pieces of good news got a flat reply.

moments.text: Emily's grandmother in hospital: Lucas cleared his week and drove
Lucas's new client, met with a groceries question
Emily's first half marathon, with a cake waiting at home

life.takeaway: The chores get done. What feels unfair is that one of you keeps track of all of them.

needs.seen: Life together feels fair to one of you, and mostly fair to the other.

evidence.insight: One of you does most of the remembering.
evidence.support: Emily sends 3 in 4 of the messages about bills, bookings and plans since 2024.

evidence.insight: Chore rows tend to start with a reminder.
evidence.support: 17 of your 23 tense exchanges about chores since 2023 began with Emily reminding Lucas of something.

needs.means: The doing is shared; the remembering is not. Emily's high conscientiousness makes her the natural tracker, and Lucas's spontaneity means he rarely thinks ahead. Being the one who always has to remind makes her feel like a manager, and makes him feel nagged.

next.do: Split the remembering, not just the doing: each of you owns a few jobs end to end, reminders included.
next.because: 17 of 23 chore rows started with a reminder from Emily.

next.do: Ten minutes on Sunday evening to look at the week together.
next.because: most chore rows start on a weekday evening, when you are both tired.

interests.means: You share cooking, music and weekends outside, and you each have a world of your own: Emily's running and books, Lucas's boat and games. Lucas needs new things and Emily needs things planned, so new things planned together suit you both.

next.do: Take turns picking one new thing to try together each month; the other plans it.
next.because: his Psyche shows he is driven by novelty, and hers by doing things well.

future.takeaway: You agree on children. Marriage and where to live are still open: talk about them before they turn into a quiet worry.

values.means: Loyalty and keeping your word are the ground you both stand on. Beyond that you pull different ways: Emily towards reliability and belonging, Lucas towards ingenuity and adventure. That shows up in small things, like how far ahead to book a holiday.

next.do: Plan one adventure a year: Lucas picks where, Emily plans how.
next.because: adventure matters to Lucas and reliability to Emily, and this uses both.

decisions.means: Children is settled. Marriage and where to live are linked: Lucas's itch for a new city fits his need for adventure, while Emily's sense of belonging is tied to where you are now. Left unspoken, this can turn into a quiet worry for the one who wants things settled.

next.do: Have one relaxed talk about where you might live in five years, with no decision needed.
next.because: you each see a different place in five years.

lines.children: You both want children one day. A good next talk is roughly when, and what needs to be in place first.
lines.marriage: One of you is sure and one is unsure. Ask what unsure means: not yet, not sure about marriage itself, or something else.
lines.place: One of you sees staying put, one sees a new city. Talk about what each place would give you, not just where it is.

growth.means: Achievement, care and freedom drive you both. You pull apart on two: Lucas needs far more novelty than Emily, and Emily needs far more security than Lucas. That is the same tension as your big decisions, a new city or staying put.

next.do: Each name one goal for next year and one way the other can help with it.
next.because: you share a drive to achieve, and back each other best when the goal is named.

secure.takeaway: You are both sure about this, and you are both reliable in a crisis. Say it out loud more often.

evidence.insight: Both of you come back after distance.
evidence.support: After 86 in 100 hard messages since 2022, one of you said something warm within a day.

attachment.means: You both lean secure, with different ways of coping. Under stress Emily handles things alone and says she's fine; Lucas starts a new project to stay busy. Neither is pulling away, but each can look like it to the other.

next.do: When you need space, say how long you need: an hour, or an evening.
next.because: Emily takes time first, and Lucas copes better when he knows when it ends.

reassure.a: Emily is reassured by an evening cleared just for her, and by being asked how she really is, twice.
reassure.b: Lucas is reassured by hearing plainly that you're okay, and that you're still with him on the plan.

security.seen: You both feel secure and sure about each other.

evidence.support: You made 14 plans more than three months ahead in 2025 and 2026, up from 3 in 2023.

security.means: This is solid ground, and it has grown: you plan further ahead now than in your first years. Feeling sure of each other is what makes harder talks, like marriage and where to live, safe to have.

next.do: Once a month, say one thing you're looking forward to doing together.
next.because: you already plan ahead; saying it out loud makes the security felt.

a: Takes on more planning than usual
b: Starts three new projects at once

disagree.takeaway: Your rows are rarely about chores or plans. They are about timing: Lucas needs to settle it now, Emily needs time first and then says it's fine.

topics.means: You each named a different topic, but they have the same root: Emily plans ahead and Lucas keeps things open. To her, his lateness feels like her time doesn't count; to him, her chore lists feel like being managed.

next.do: Agree three simple house rules: who books, who tidies what, and how late is too late.
next.because: both topics keep coming back in the messages.

cycle.means: This is a common loop, and it can be fixed. Lucas's push to settle things and Emily's habit of smoothing them over each make sense alone; together, they bury the issue instead of solving it.

next.do: Agree on a phrase that means: I need an hour, and I will come back to this.
next.because: Emily needs time first, and Lucas needs to know the talk will happen.

steps: Something small goes wrong, often about plans or chores
Lucas wants to talk it through now
Emily says it's fine, to keep the peace
It comes back later, bigger, and Lucas feels blindsided

plain.a: When Emily says it's fine quickly, she needs time to think and to feel safe saying what's wrong. Next time, she can ask for an hour, then come back and say it plainly.
plain.b: When Lucas sends message after message, he needs to know you're still in it together. Next time, he can say it once, then give Emily the hour she asks for.

disagreements.seen: Getting past disagreements feels harder to one of you than to the other.

evidence.insight: Repairs mostly land, and faster every year.
evidence.support: Of 41 repair attempts after friction, 33 were taken up. Getting back to warm took about 6 hours in 2023 and about 3.5 hours since 2025.

evidence.insight: What isn't repaired is what was never said.
evidence.support: 9 of 23 chore rows reopened an earlier one that had ended with Emily saying it was fine.

disagreements.means: You are good at making up: a joke from Lucas or a kind message from Emily usually works. The trouble is what gets smoothed over instead of settled. Repairing the row is not the same as solving what caused it.

next.do: After a row, send one warm line within the hour, even if the talk comes later.
next.because: most repairs land; the long wait before them is what hurts.

next.do: Emily: name a time to come back to it. Lucas: trust that time and wait.
next.because: one of you needs time first, the other needs to talk now.

overall.title: How you feel about it all
overall.detail: You are each happier in this than the other one guesses. Tell each other plainly what is going well, and you will both worry less.

intermission.title: Your story in small moments
lines: Your longest streak: 403 days in a row of messages.
Emily sends the plans. Lucas sends plan B.
Your busiest day was 14 May 2022: 212 messages.
You end most nights with the same silly goodnight.

week1.title: Small daily turns
days: Lucas: thank Emily for the work behind one thing she did today.
Phones away for the first 20 minutes of dinner.
When good news comes in, ask two questions before changing the subject.
Each do one job the other usually keeps track of, start to finish.
Send an afternoon message that has nothing to do with logistics.
Emily: say one thing you need this week, out loud.
Lucas plans an evening for two with nothing after it.

weeks.title: Week 2: the gap after a row

conversation.title: Talk now, or time first
conversation.why: It's the loop behind most of your rows.
script: Pick a calm evening, not right after a row.
Each say what you need right after a disagreement.
Agree a phrase for: I need an hour, and I'll come back.
Agree how long is okay, and what the warm line in between looks like.

weeks.ask: When I say it's fine, how can you tell if it really is?
weeks.doTogether: Try your new phrase the next time something small goes wrong.

weeks.title: Week 3: the invisible load

conversation.title: Who keeps track of what
conversation.why: The remembering, not the doing, is what feels unfair.
script: List everything that needs remembering at home.
Each pick the jobs you'll own, start to finish, reminders included.
Check in after a week on what slipped.

weeks.ask: What do I do that you'd miss if I stopped?
weeks.doTogether: Spend ten minutes on Sunday evening looking at the week ahead.

weeks.title: Week 4: what comes next

conversation.title: Five years from now
conversation.why: Where to live and when to marry are still open.
script: Each describe an ordinary Tuesday in five years.
Notice what's the same in both.
Pick one small step toward it.

weeks.ask: What would help you feel sure about the next big step?
weeks.doTogether: Spend a weekend away somewhere you might like to live one day.

caveats: This reads your messages, your answers and your two Psyches. It can't see your days together, your tone of voice or anything you only say in person.
